caption:
France's rail network reached about 42,000 km in the 1930s. Today it is down to roughly 29,000 km.

Watch it draw itself at its real construction dates — the 1827 coal line out of Saint-Étienne, the star of main lines radiating from Paris, then the secondary lines of the 1880s reaching almost every subprefecture. After the 1930s peak the map thins out: branch lines close, tracks are lifted.

📊 Each section appears the year it opened and fades the year it closed to all traffic. The dataset was rebuilt for this video: track geometry from SNCF Réseau's national network file (closed and sold-off lines included) and from OpenStreetMap for lines since dismantled; opening and closing dates read from the French Wikipedia article of each line, completed by OpenHistoricalMap. It covers about 37,000 km of the roughly 42,000 km peak — narrow-gauge local networks are out of scope and some dates are approximate.

Source: SNCF Réseau (ODbL) · OpenStreetMap (ODbL) · Wikipédia FR (CC BY-SA) · OpenHistoricalMap (ODbL) · land: Natural Earth.
